dossiers.label: The sail and the third man
dossiers.about: Young Socrates meets old Parmenides. Is the whole form in each thing, like one day in many places? Rather like a sail spread over many people, Parmenides says, a part over each. And if one sees the large itself and the large things together, another largeness will appear, and another: no longer one form, but infinitely many.

passage.start_quote: οἷον [εἰ] ἡμέρα [εἴη] μία καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ οὖσα πολλαχοῦ ἅμα ἐστὶ

parts.label: Like one day in many places
parts.quote: ἡμέρα [εἴη] μία καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ οὖσα πολλαχοῦ ἅμα ἐστὶ

parts.label: Like a sail spread over many people
parts.quote: οἷον εἰ ἱστίῳ καταπετάσας πολλοὺς ἀνθρώπους

parts.label: One form over many large things
parts.quote: μία τις ἴσως δοκεῖ ἰδέα ἡ αὐτὴ εἶναι ἐπὶ πάντα ἰδόντι

parts.label: Another form of largeness will appear
Perhaps forms are thoughts in souls?
parts.quote: μὴ τῶν εἰδῶν ἕκαστον ᾖ τούτων νόημα

echoes.why: The Republic's beds: if god made two, a third would appear whose form they both had.

related.why: The Republic's own regress argument: god made only one bed.

web.title: Parmenides (dialogue)
web.quote: Parmenides presses Socrates on how, precisely, many particulars can participate in a single Form
